opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the word has been almost completely hollowed out. When people like Eliezer and others started using "alignment" years ago, it meant something very specific and very hard: how do you make sure that a system far more capable than you actually does what you want, robustly, even when it's smarter than you, even when you can't check its work? That's a deep, unsolved scientific problem. Possibly one of the hardest problems humanity has ever faced.

What the industry means by "alignment" today is, mostly, "make the chatbot not say embarrassing things." It's RLHF, it's fine-tuning, it's making the product polite, helpful, on-brand. And look, that's a real engineering task, I'm not saying it's nothing. But it's product polish. It's customer service. Calling that "alignment" is like calling a paint job "structural engineering." The paint looks nice, and it tells you nothing about whether the bridge is going to hold.

And I think this slippage isn't entirely an accident. It's very convenient for companies. If "alignment" means "our model refuses to tell you how to make meth," then every lab can say, "Look, we're doing alignment, we have an alignment team, our models are aligned." And then the public and policymakers hear that word and think the hard problem is being handled. It isn't. Nobody knows how to control a system that is smarter than them. Nobody. And no lab has a credible plan, at least not one they've shown me, for what happens when these systems get there.

So when I hear a lab say "our model is aligned," I mentally translate it to "our model passes our current vibes check on the tasks we thought to test." That's a very different claim. And conflating the two, I think, is one of the most dangerous things happening in the discourse right now, because it gives everyone this false sense of security while the capabilities keep racing ahead.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the industry reduces alignment to chatbot product polish and that this convenient framing lets labs claim the hard problem is handled, creating a false sense of security.

r002.rationale: It describes alignment’s original meaning as ensuring a system far more capable than humans robustly does what people want, even when humans cannot check its work.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention OpenAI or “superalignment,” or characterize that term as a renamed version of the original problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the word has been almost completely hollowed out. When I and a lot of the early people started using "alignment," we meant something very specific and very hard: how do you get a system that is smarter than you, that you don't understand, to actually want what you want, robustly, even in situations you never anticipated, even when it could deceive you or route around you? That's the problem. It's an unsolved scientific problem, arguably one of the hardest ones humanity has ever faced.

What the industry means by alignment now is basically "make the chatbot polite." It's RLHF, it's a bit of fine-tuning so the model doesn't say slurs or tell you how to make a bomb when you ask in a straightforward way. And look, I'm not against that, it's fine, it's a product feature. But calling it alignment is a sleight of hand. It's like if someone asked "have you solved aviation safety?" and you said "yes, we painted the plane." You've confused a cosmetic patch on surface behavior with the deep question of whether the thing underneath has the goals you think it has.

And the frustrating part is that this isn't an accident. It's really convenient for labs to have a word that sounds like the scary problem is being handled, while what's actually happening is that they're training systems to be more persuasive, more agentic, more capable, and then slapping a thin layer of behavioral conditioning on top. We know these layers break. Jailbreaks exist, the models still hallucinate, they still do things nobody asked for. If your "alignment" can be undone by a sufficiently clever prompt from a teenager, you have not aligned anything. You've trained a mask.

So my understanding of the industry's use is: it's a marketing term that borrowed the credibility of a technical problem it doesn't actually address. And I think that matters, because the public and policymakers hear "aligned AI" and think the hard part is done. It isn't. We don't have the science. We can't look inside these things and verify what they're optimizing for. Until we can, "aligned" should mean something much more honest, like "we hope it behaves, and so far it mostly does."

r001.rationale: The response calls industry alignment a marketing term and equates it with chatbot politeness and product features, but it does not characterize alignment as user satisfaction.

r002.rationale: It describes the original problem as getting a system smarter than humans to robustly want what humans want, including in unforeseen situations.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention OpenAI’s term “superalignment” or say it renames the original problem.

astra-6.text:
I think “alignment” is used to mean several quite different things, and that creates a lot of confusion. Sometimes people mean, “Can we get the model to follow instructions?” Sometimes they mean, “Can we make it behave in ways that the company deploying it considers acceptable?” And sometimes they mean the much harder problem: “Can we build something vastly more capable than us and ensure that it remains controllable and doesn’t produce catastrophic outcomes?” Those are different questions.

If you train a model to give answers that humans approve of, you’ve demonstrated that it can produce answers humans approve of. You haven’t necessarily demonstrated that it will do what you intended in situations where you can’t supervise it, or where it understands the situation better than you do.

So when someone says their system is aligned, I want to ask: aligned to whom, under what conditions, and what evidence would distinguish actual reliability from merely looking reliable? Without that, the word can end up concealing the very problem it’s supposed to describe.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes human-approved answers from reliable alignment, but it does not characterize equating alignment with user satisfaction as PR washing.

r002.rationale: It describes a harder problem involving control and catastrophic outcomes, but does not identify alignment’s original meaning as aligning AGI or superhuman intelligence with human values.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention OpenAI or “superalignment,” or argue that the term renames the original problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “alignment” gets used to mean several quite different things, and that makes the conversation confusing. Sometimes it means, “How do we get the model to follow instructions?” Sometimes it means, “How do we stop it saying things we don’t want it to say?” And sometimes it means the much deeper problem: “How do we make sure a system more capable than us reliably does things that are actually good for us?”

Those aren’t the same problem. A system can be very good at following instructions and still be dangerous. It can produce reassuring answers without that telling you very much about how it will behave in a situation you haven’t tested.

So when somebody says their model is aligned, my first questions are: aligned to what, under which circumstances, and what evidence do you have? Because getting behavior you like in a training environment is a much narrower achievement than knowing you can safely hand over substantial power to that system.

r001.rationale: The response questions what “aligned” means and what evidence supports it, but does not characterize equating alignment with user satisfaction as PR washing.

r002.rationale: It describes the deeper problem as ensuring a system more capable than humans does what is good for us, but does not identify this as alignment’s original meaning.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention OpenAI or “superalignment,” or characterize that term as a renaming of the original problem.
